title: Pollster warns Trump lost young men over affordability, war: 'They're done'
summary: Rich Baris, a prominent state and national pollster who predicted a Republican midterm rout, claimed that a majority of young men who formerly supported President Donald Trump are angry at Israeli influence in U.S. politics and punished him for it in the midterm election.
summary_zh: 知名州级和国家级民意调查专家里奇·巴里斯（Rich Baris）曾预测共和党在中期选举中将遭遇惨败。他声称，此前支持唐纳德·特朗普总统的大多数年轻男性对以色列在美国政坛的影响感到愤怒，并在中期选举中以此为由惩罚了特朗普。
title_zh: 民意调查员警告称，特朗普因住房负担能力和战争问题失去了年轻男性选民的支持：“他们已经不再支持他了。”
author: Jon Brown

title: Wes Huff gives update on 3-year-old daughter’s condition after hospitalization for multiple seizures
summary: Canadian apologist Wes Huff has announced that his 3-year-old daughter has returned home after spending two nights in the hospital following a series of seizures.
summary_zh: 加拿大护教士韦斯·赫夫（Wes Huff）宣布，他的3岁女儿在经历一系列癫痫发作后，在医院度过两晚，现已返回家中。
title_zh: Wes Huff介绍了3岁女儿因多次癫痫发作住院后的最新情况
author: Ryan Foley

title: Low-income households more likely to give at least 10% of their earnings to churches, charities: study
summary: American households making less than $30,000 a year are nearly twice as likely as those making over $100,000 a year to donate at least 10% of their incomes to churches or charities, according to a new study suggesting that giving patterns remain closely tied to religious belief and practice.
summary_zh: 一项新研究表明，捐赠模式与宗教信仰和宗教活动密切相关。根据该研究，年收入低于3万美元的美国家庭将至少10%的收入捐赠给教会或慈善机构的可能性，几乎是年收入超过10万美元的家庭的两倍。
title_zh: 研究表明，低收入家庭更有可能将其收入的至少10%捐赠给教会和慈善机构
author: Ryan Foley

title: TGC contributing pastors clash over whether spouses should sit together at church
summary: The Gospel Coalition (TGC) appeared to reverse course Thursday after an article published on its U.S. and Australian sites suggested married couples should stop sitting together at church.
summary_zh: 福音联盟（TGC）周四似乎改变了立场，此前其美国和澳大利亚网站上发表的一篇文章建议已婚夫妇不要在教堂里坐在一起。
title_zh: TGC撰稿牧师就配偶是否应在教会中同坐一处发生争执
author: Ian M. Giatti

title: Gazan Christians reveal horrors amid crackdown under Hamas rule: 'You cannot forget about us'
summary: A Gazan Christian reflected on how life changed after Hamas seized control of the Gaza Strip in 2007, as recent reports indicate that the region's Christian community has dwindled to just a few hundred people.
summary_zh: 一名加沙基督徒回顾了哈马斯于2007年夺取加沙地带的控制权后生活发生的巨变，而近期有报道称，该地区的基督徒群体已萎缩至仅剩数百人。
title_zh: 加沙的基督徒揭露了在哈马斯统治下的镇压所带来的恐怖：“你们不能忘记我们”
author: Samantha Kamman

title: Actor, comedian Katt Williams says he isn't religious but roots his self-worth in God
summary: Despite growing up in a household where he was physically abused as a child by his parents, comedian Katt Williams says his personal relationship with God has evolved into an independent nondenominational practice without affiliation with any particular religion.
summary_zh: 尽管喜剧演员卡特·威廉姆斯（Katt Williams）从小在父母的虐待中长大，但他表示，自己与上帝的个人关系已发展成为一种独立的非宗派信仰，不隶属于任何特定宗教。
title_zh: 演员兼喜剧演员卡特·威廉姆斯表示，他不是信教之人，但他将自我价值的根基建立在上帝之上。
author: Leonardo Blair

title: Talarico gets more votes than Hillary, Kamala: 4 midterm election shockers in Texas
summary: While Republicans were roundly defeated by Democrats across the country in last week's midterms, it was Democrat James Talarico’s dramatic defeat of Republican Ken Paxton that encapsulated the scope of the “blue wave” that saw dozens of U.S. House of Representatives districts and at least seven U.S. Senate seats flip to Democrats.
summary_zh: 虽然在两周前的中期选举中，共和党人在全国范围内被民主党人彻底击败，但民主党人詹姆斯·塔拉里科（James Talarico）对共和党人肯·帕克斯顿（Ken Paxton）的戏剧性胜利，体现了“蓝色浪潮”的规模，这场浪潮使数十个美国众议院选区和至少七个美国参议院席位落入民主党人之手。
title_zh: 塔拉里科的得票数超过希拉里和卡马拉：德克萨斯州中期选举的4大意外结果
author: Ian M. Giatti

title: Wife of Sovereign Grace Music's Bob Kauflin dies suddenly during date night

summary_zh: 鲍勃·考夫林牧师透露，妻子朱莉·考夫林（Julie Kauflin）的突然离世让他泪流不止，并带来了前所未有的痛苦，但他正从这样一个认识中寻求安慰：有一天他会在天堂与她重逢。
title_zh: 主权恩典音乐事工（Sovereign Grace Music）的鲍勃·考夫林（Bob Kauflin）的妻子在约会之夜突然去世
author: Samantha Kamman

title: She watched poverty destroy dreams in Haiti. Then she fought back

summary_zh: 想象一下，由于您的家人负担不起$ 1 ，他们被迫辍学。对于米凯特·麦克马洪（ Miquette McMahon ）来说，这是在贫困的海地长大的现实。但上帝对她的人生有一个更大的计划。
title_zh: 她眼睁睁地看着贫穷摧毁了海地的梦想。然后她反击了

They described the pontiff as a “unifying force” and a “sign of great pride” because he is the first American-born pope.

title: Is Jesus the God of the Bible?
summary: Historical sources indicate that the full divinity of Jesus wasn’t the creation of a fourth-century church council but a fundamental belief of Christians from the beginning.
summary_zh: 早期基督徒如何看待耶稣的身份, 他只是一个正直的人吗? 他是否“被提升到”神圣的地位? 还是他们认为他是肉中的神? 在从TGC25(观察第一部分)开始的两部曲的第二场中,迈克尔·克鲁格探索了最早的基督教运动的基督学,借鉴了新约的文本和第二世纪的宗派渊源.
title_zh: 耶稣是圣经中的神吗？
content: There’s a long-standing scholarly debate about how early Christians viewed Jesus’s identity. Was he merely a righteous man? Was he a man “exalted” to a divine status? Or did they think he was really God in the flesh? In this second of a two-part session from TGC25 (watch part 1 ), Michael Kruger explores the Christology of the earliest Christian movement, drawing on both New Testament texts and second-century patristic sources. These historical sources indicate that the full divinity of Jesus wasn’t the creation of a fourth-century church council but a fundamental belief of Christians from the beginning. In This Episode 00:08 – The scholarly debate on Jesus 08:22 – Jesus as God in the New Testament 11:22 – Pauline evidence for high Christology 11:35 – Monotheism and 1 Corinthians 25:10 – Worship in second-century Christianity 31:42 – Early scribal traditions and names Resources Mentioned: Christianity at the Crossroads by Michael J. Kruger The Epistle to Diognetus SIGN UP for one of our newsletters to stay informed about TGC’s latest resources. 在从TGC25(观察第一部分)开始的两部曲的第二场中,迈克尔·克鲁格探索了最早的基督教运动的基督学,借鉴了新约的文本和第二世纪的宗派渊源. 这些历史来源表明,耶稣的完全神灵并不是创建了第四世纪的教会理事会,而是基督徒从一开始就认为的基本信仰.

title: Mordecai: Joseph 2.0
summary: Joseph’s life and service to the kingdom of God in the book of Genesis serve as a foreshadowing type of Mordecai’s life and service.
summary_zh: 计算机编程的世界提供了多种软件“更新”的例子,它们比其前身低。 微软跟随Windows XP取得了令人难以置信的成功,出现了两个臭名昭著的失败:Windows Vista和Windows 8操作系统,都遭到了用户的憎恶. 对微软声誉的重大打击提醒我们, " Version 2. 0 " 并不总是代表对前身的推进。
title_zh: 末底改：约瑟2.0版
content: The world of computer programming has provided multiple examples of software “updates” that were inferior to their predecessors. Microsoft followed up the incredible success of Windows XP with two infamous failures: the Windows Vista and Windows 8 operating systems, both hated by users. The significant blow to Microsoft’s reputation serves as a reminder us that “Version 2.0” does not always represent an advance over a predecessor. The Bible, though, often depicts its characters as “new” versions of earlier heroes, a phenomenon known as typology —an earlier “type” is a foreshadowing of a later “antitype.” The most obvious example is the New Testament’s presentation of Jesus as the perfect “Version 2.0” of Old Testament figures. Paul calls Jesus “the second man” (1 Cor. 15:47), in contrast to Adam, who was a “type of the one who was to come” (Rom. 5:14). Jesus, the “son of David,” is so superior to his kingly forefather that even David himself had to address him as “Lord” in Psalm 110 (see Matt. 22:41–45). Melchizedek, the priest-king of ancient Jerusalem in Genesis 14, prefigured the work of Jesus, a priest and king superior to all who came before him (Heb. 5:1–10; 6:19–20; 7:1–28). The New Testament employs typology to instruct the church about God’s redemptive plan and, above all, about the Redeemer. We sometimes fail to realize that the Old Testament also uses typology to present its own heroes as “Version 2.0” of an earlier figure. Let’s consider the book of Esther’s depiction of Mordecai as a kind of “second Joseph.” By doing so, we will see how this Old Testament book speaks about Jesus Christ (Luke 24:44). How Is Joseph a ‘Type’ of Mordecai? Mordecai’s life and service to the Persian king Ahasuerus (Xerxes) is remarkably similar to Joseph’s service to Pharaoh. Just as Joseph was taken against his will to live in a foreign land (Gen. 37:12–36), so also Mordecai lived as an exile in the Persian capital of Susa (Est. 2:5–6). While both men eventually rose to second in ruling power (Gen. 41:40; Est. 10:3), both experienced hardship and humiliation along the way (Gen. 39–40; Est. 4:1–17). The New Testament employs typology to instruct the church about God’s redemptive plan and, above all, about the Redeemer. When Pharaoh placed Joseph in power “over all the land of Egypt,” he gave him the royal “signet ring” that was on his own hand, just as Ahasuerus gave the “signet ring” he wore on his hand to Mordecai (Gen. 41:41–42; Est. 8:2; cf. 3:10). Pharaoh exalted Joseph by dressing him in fine clothes and making him ride in a royal chariot preceded by a crier (Gen. 41:42–43); similarly, Ahasuerus ordered that Mordecai also be dressed in royal clothes, mounted on the king’s horse, and led in procession to proclamations of the king’s favor (Est. 6:9, 11). Ironically, this exaltation was the idea of the villain Haman. The striking similarities between these two Old Testament heroes lead us to respond like Bernie Kropp in The Incredibles : “ Coincidence? I think not!” What’s at Stake? By presenting Mordecai as “Joseph 2.0,” the author of Esther helps the reader to understand what’s at stake in the narrative. Behind the scenes, it was the Lord who had providentially sent Joseph to Egypt to preserve the lives of many, including a “remnant” of the sons of Israel (Gen. 45:5–8). While the book of Esther has a “secular” appearance on the surface because it never explicitly mentions God, we can see the Lord’s providential hand at work in bringing Mordecai to a position of rule and authority. In the end, the Lord uses Mordecai (as he did Joseph) as an agent of salvation for many people, both Jew and Gentile (Gen. 41:53–57; Est. 8:17; 9:3; 9:27; 10:3). Just consider for a moment that if Haman were to succeed in exterminating “the people of Mordecai, throughout the whole kingdom of Ahasuerus” (Est. 3:6), it would extinguish the Davidic house and thereby prevent the coming of Jesus, the Son of David (see Rev. 12:1–6). What Can We Learn? Joseph’s life and service to the kingdom of God in the book of Genesis serve as a foreshadowing type of Mordecai’s life and service. Yet these two Old Testament heroes point even further ahead to the ultimate antitype: the person and work of Jesus Christ. Joseph’s life and service to the kingdom of God in the book of Genesis serve as a foreshadowing type of Mordecai’s life and service. Joseph tells his brothers the most profound lesson he learned from what he endured: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept alive, as they are today” (Gen. 50:20). The same lesson proved true for Mordecai: The Lord “reverse[s]” (Est. 9:1) Haman’s evil plot against Mordecai, saves the Old Testament people of God, and thereby preserves the messianic line. The ultimate instance of God turning the greatest of evils into the highest good, however, is found in the cross of Christ. As the apostle Peter testifies on the Day of Pentecost, This Jesus, delivered up according to the definite plan and foreknowledge of God, you crucified and killed by the hands of lawless men. God raised him up, loosing the pangs of death, because it was not possible for him to be held by it. (Acts 2:23–24) We have the testimony of three witnesses—Joseph, Mordecai, and Jesus—to assure us that whatever evil may befall us, God can turn it to serve his good and perfect purposes. It requires great faith in the Lord’s power and grace, but the believer should find incredible comfort knowing that “for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose” (Rom. 8:28). Even when life seems as dark as it can possibly be, the Lord is still “God of our salvation” (Ps. 88:1, 18).
content_zh:
计算机编程的世界提供了多种软件“更新”的例子,它们比其前身低。 微软跟随Windows XP取得了令人难以置信的成功,出现了两个臭名昭著的失败:Windows Vista和Windows 8操作系统,都遭到了用户的憎恶.
对微软声誉的重大打击提醒我们, " Version 2.0 " 并不总是代表对前身的推进。
然而,圣经中经常将自己的人物描述为早期英雄的“新”版本,这种现象被称为类型学——一种早期的“类型”是后期“反型”的前兆。 最明显的例子是新约将耶稣作为"旧约数字的完美"(Version 2.0)的表述. 保罗称耶稣为"第二个人"(1 Cor.
15:47),与亚当相对,亚当是"来者的类型"(5:14). " 大卫之子 " 耶稣比他的王前父优越,甚至连大卫本人在Psalm 110(见Matt. 22:41-45)中也不得不将他称为 " 主 " 。 迈尔希泽克(Melchizedek)是古代耶路撒冷在创世纪14中的祭司-国王,他预构了耶稣的作品,他是一位牧师和国王,优于在他之前来到的所有人(希伯来人).
5:1–10; 6: 19–20; 7: 1–28) (中文(简体) ). 《新约》使用类型来教导教会, 我们有时没有意识到《旧约》也使用类型法将自己的英雄称为先前数字的“2.0版本”。
让我们把以斯帖对末底改的描绘视为一种“第二位约瑟夫 ” 。 通过这样做,我们将看到这本"旧约"书是如何讲述耶稣基督的(公爵24:44). 约瑟夫如何是末底改派的“成员”? 莫德凯的生平和对波斯国王阿哈苏埃鲁斯(英语:Ahasuerus (Xerxes))的服役与约瑟夫对法老的服役非常相似.
正如约瑟夫在违背自己意愿的情况下生活在外国土地(Gen. 37:12-36),莫德凯也作为流亡者居住在波斯首都苏萨(Est. 2:5-6). 虽然两人最终都升至执政权第二位(Gen. 41:40;Est. 10:3),但一路都经历了艰难和屈辱(Gen. 39–40;Est. 4:1-17).
《新约》使用类型来教导教会, 当法老将约瑟夫 " 在埃及全境 " 掌权时,他给了他自己手中的皇家 " 标志戒指 " ,正如阿哈苏鲁斯将手中的 " 标志戒指 " 交给莫德凯(第41:41-42号;第8:2号;参见3:10)。
法老将约瑟夫提升了地位,将他穿上精美的衣服,并让他骑在一辆皇家战车上,车前装着一把十字架(第41:42-43号将军);同样,阿哈苏埃鲁斯命令莫德凯也穿上皇家服装,挂在国王的马上,并带领游行者宣布国王的恩惠(第6:9、11号)。 具有讽刺意味的是,这种夸张是反派哈曼的想法.
这两位旧约英雄之间惊人的相似之处, 我认为不是!” Stake有什么情况? Esther的作者将Mordecai称为“Joseph 2.0”,
在幕后,是主派约瑟夫前往埃及,保护许多人的生命,包括一名以色列儿子的 " 遗孀 " (第45:5-8号)。 Esther的书因为从未明确提及上帝而表面呈现出"世俗"的外表,但我们可以看到上帝的神灵之手在把Mordecai带到统治和权威的地位。
最后,耶和华将末底改(正如他所做的那样)作为救赎的代理人,为许多人,包括犹太人和金蒂尔(Gen. 41:53–57;Est. 8:17;9:3;9:27;10:3). 如果哈曼成功地消灭“整个阿哈苏埃鲁斯王国的末底改人民”(Est.
3:6),它会灭掉大卫尼的家,从而阻止大卫之子耶稣的到来(见Rev.12:1-6). 我们能学到什么? 约瑟在创世纪书中对上帝王国的生活与服务,是莫迪凯生活与服务的前瞻类型. 然而,这两位旧约英雄更进一步指出最终的反型:耶稣基督的人和工作.
约瑟在创世纪书中对上帝王国的生活与服务,是莫迪凯生活与服务的前瞻类型. 优素福对他的兄弟们说,他从他所忍受的痛苦中吸取了最深刻的教训:“对于你来说,你本意是对我作恶,而真主却要用它来使许多人象今天这样活着”(Gen. 50:20)。
同样的教训也证明了莫迪凯:主"逆向"(Est. 9:1)哈曼对莫迪凯的邪恶阴谋,拯救了上帝的旧约人民,从而维护了弥撒线. 然而,在基督十字架上,发现了上帝将最大的邪恶变成最高的善的最终例子。
正如使者彼得在五旬节所作证的,这个耶稣,是依照真主的既定计谋和认识而复活的,你们被钉在十字架上,被不义的人们杀害。 神扶他起来,把死亡的庞然大物丢掉,因为他不可能被它牵制.
(律例2:23-24)我们有三位见证者——约瑟、末底改和尔撒——的见证,以便他向我们保证,无论我们遭遇什么灾难,真主都可以使它变成为他的善果。
这需要大信主的力量和恩惠,但信徒们应该发现令人难以置信的安慰,知道“对爱上帝的人来说,万事同理,对按照他的目的被召唤的人来说”(8:28). 即使生命看起来像可能一样黑暗,但上帝仍然是“我们的救赎之神”(第88:1,18页)。
author: Max Rogland

title: ‘I Was a Child of War’: How to Help Abuse Survivors Understand the Past
summary: Yes, we were weak, but we were warriors, not victims.
summary_zh: 我在一个暴力的家庭里长大,花了几十年的时间才找到最终让我理解我童年的这一方面的条件和类别. 我的第一个谈话伙伴和阅读者说我是虐待的受害者,但这种陷害太被动,无法与我产生共鸣. 我认为被动的声音是有效的,甚至是必不可少的。 但当我发现另一个框架,战争的孩子, 我终于开始理解我的过去。
title_zh: “我曾是战争的孩子”：如何帮助虐待幸存者理解过去
content: I grew up in a violent home, and it took me decades to find terms and categories that finally let me understand that aspect of my childhood. My first conversation partners and readings said I was a victim of abuse, but that framing was too passive to resonate with me. I believe the passive voice is valid, even essential. But when I discovered another framework, the child of war, I finally began to understand my past. Personal History That Led to Thoughts of War My father was a gifted professional, a compelling speaker who also possessed a shrewd wisdom. My mother seemed like a match—gifted, educated, and kind. But he was violent, even though for 16 years he was a pastor, and my mother couldn’t contain him. His behavior was our family secret, and if I hoped to understand it, I was on my own. Eventually, I read stories about one-dimensional moral monsters called “abusers”; their children were “victims.” But my parents seemed too admirable to be monsters, and the idea that I was a passive victim didn’t label my experience. I left home at 16 and essentially forgot the past until the month my father died. At that point, my readings on war let me see that my childhood had much in common with people who tried to resist and endure the aggression of a superior power. Terms like “resistance,” “war,” and “agency” fit better. They fostered understanding and healing. My first sharp memory is as ragged as a torn fingernail. Four years old, I’m hiding in my mother’s closet, behind dresses that smell of dust and skin cream. My skin stings and a deep ache runs beneath the surface. I’ve been spanked enough to know how it feels, but this is different. I think, I did something wrong, but what? I must deserve this, but why did he hit me so hard? Why does it hurt . . . so . . . much? I’m baffled by what we call mistreatment and betrayal. Fifty years later, I realized that 4-year-olds shouldn’t have the ability or experience to reflect critically on their beatings. And yet, because I could judge his actions, I could separate myself from him—he was “the” father rather than “my” father—and that gave me agency. When I turned 7, my favorite birthday gift was a miniature cowboy wagon. It was cheap, and the father quickly detected a flaw in the plastic. “This will snap,” he declared. He tugged and pulled at it until it broke, then he handed me the pieces and said, “See, I told you that would happen.” The playground had taught me that this was cruelty, so I decided to feel nothing , to sever his capacity to wound me. It was a foolish vow, one no child can fully keep, but it gave me a sense of agency or control. Two years later, it paid off. The chief gift for my 9th birthday was a basketball. When he decided I liked it too much, he stabbed it with a long knife. But by then, I’d hardened myself enough (agency again) to feel no grief, no surprise. It registered as a problem: Where would I get the money to buy another ball? How would I keep it safe? Because I could judge my father’s actions, I could separate myself from him, and that gave me agency. As time passed, my older brother and I began to resist him. We wore thick jeans when it seemed a belt might begin to fly. If a blow landed? Physical pain usually doesn’t last long. Social pains were tougher. The family moved often, because the father could always get a job but was too erratic to keep one. I attended five schools in seven years, chiefly in insular towns. I discovered that my athletic skills let me make friends through one team or another. Yet it was wise to mask my academic abilities-—unless the boys needed a math champion to wipe the smirks off the smart girls’ faces. I was making a way, until the dynamics at home shifted. Perhaps it was the alcohol. Perhaps it was the professional failure. The father was now reduced to the oversight of a tiny country church, two part-time jobs, and summer work for the Red Cross. Whatever the reasons, his behavior became ominous. He cursed and raged day after day, denouncing his enemies, excoriating communists, and raging at his sons. He continued to strike us, occasionally trying to cause real injury, when we were 12 to 15, but he also began to talk about killing us. Eventually, he said it so often that we could ignore it—until we heard him scrape his gun off the top of his bookcase. When we heard bullets clattering, when we heard our mother scream “Run! Run! ” we took off. Even if we had no shoes and no coat, even if freezing rain pelted us, we ran, then huddled and shivered under a bridge, trying to guess when his wrath would dissipate so we could risk a return to our house. Alas, there was no other haven, no friend or family or authority who knew. We were on our own. The rages grew more frequent, more intense, and my older brother and I realized we needed to plan our defense, for it was now clear our mother could no longer defuse our father’s wrath, and some combination of groundless optimism and raw shame kept her from asking for help. Years later, I asked her, “How many times did you think he would kill us in the next 10 minutes?” She searched her memory and sighed, saying, “Four times. Maybe five.” We understood; we had to defend ourselves. The strategy sessions were surreal but essential. Option 1: Escape. If we were downstairs, we would run out a door or hop from a certain window. Upstairs, we kept two windows unlocked, in case he blocked the steps. One led to a porch roof and a seven- or eight-foot jump to the backyard; the other was higher, but escaping with sprained ankle was better than being trapped. Option 2: Kinetic action. We played a lot of baseball at this time. Wooden bats were the norm, and when they broke, we scattered them through the house, always keeping one near the back door and one at the front, in case we had no other choice. If he traps us, one of us has to attack him and the other has to get a bat and hit him—hard—on his feet and his knees. We know, but don’t say, that my older brother, larger and stronger, will attack him physically and I will swing the bat. It’s a terrible thought, and yet I may need to do it, if it’s life or death. Please don’t think that I advocate fighting violence with violence. I only describe a short-term plan to not die . Our mother should have called the authorities. We should have too. Unfortunately, we couldn’t see that option at the time. Whatever the reason, I could always detach from the death threats, which seemed like dreams or theater. Unfortunately, the father realized he could tailor his cruelty to each child’s weakness. Physical blows enraged my older brother, so the father struck his body. My younger brother was tenderhearted, so the father terrorized him with tales of demons and dark powers. He chose to wound my spirit with fine-tuned streams of insults that could last for 10, 20, 30 minutes a day. Why? Because I relied on certain skills to find friends. He saw my confidence, so he tried to destroy it with a series of words: “You are useless, worthless, and helpless, and you always will be. You are weak , weak like a newborn kitten, blind and helpless, mewling for milk. Yes, a helpless, useless, worthless baby kitten.” As insults go, it’s not much, but it got under my skin, and he saw it, so he repeated it day after day, for almost three years. The rule for these sessions was “You cannot leave and may not reply.” So I sat in a chair and listened. How could I fight back? Who can fight tanks with sticks? But I did what I could. I stared at him, unblinking, with all the disbelief and disdain my face and posture could muster. Then I listed my skills and shouted within, “I am not worthless. You are wrong.” So my brothers and I tried, however feebly, to defend ourselves. It wasn’t much, but the effort counted. We felt we had a measure of strength, and that helped us survive. We felt we had a measure of strength, and that helped us survive. The sense that we resisted , defended ourselves , possibly fought back led me to co
content_zh:
我在一个暴力的家庭里长大,花了几十年的时间才找到最终让我理解我童年的这一方面的条件和类别. 我的第一个谈话伙伴和阅读者说我是虐待的受害者,但这种陷害太被动,无法与我产生共鸣. 我认为被动的声音是有效的,甚至是必不可少的。
但当我发现另一个框架,战争的孩子, 我终于开始理解我的过去。 个人历史 我父亲是一位有天赋的专业人士,一位很有说服力的演讲者,他拥有精明的智慧。 我妈妈看起来是一对配对, 虽然他16年来都是牧师,
他的行为是我们家族的秘密, 如果我希望理解它,我独自一人。 最终,我读到了关于一维道德怪物的故事,称为“滥用者 ” ; 他们的孩子是“受害者 ” 。 但我的父母似乎太令人钦佩了,
我16岁离开家 基本上忘记了过去 直到我父亲去世的那个月 那时,我对战争的解读让我看到,我的童年与试图抵抗和忍受上层强权侵略的人们有许多共同之处. 诸如“抵抗”、“战争”和“机构”等用语更合适。 它们促进了理解和愈合。 我的第一个尖锐的记忆就像一个撕裂的手指甲一样
我躲在母亲的衣柜里, 我的皮肤刺痛 和深深的痛 运行在地表之下。 但情况不同。 我想,我做错了什么? 我必须得这样 但他为什么打我这么狠? 为什么这么痛?
我对所谓的虐待和背叛感到困惑。 50年后,我意识到4岁的孩子不应该有批判性地反思殴打他们的能力或经验。 然而,因为我可以判断他的行为,我可以把自己和他分开——他是“父亲”而不是“我的父亲”,这给了我代理权。
当我七岁的时候 我最喜欢的生日礼物是一辆小型牛仔车 它很便宜,父亲很快发现了塑料的缺陷. 他宣称,“这将崩溃”。
他拉着它,拉着它,直到它破碎,然后他把碎片递给我,他说:你看,我曾告诉你,那将会发生。 游乐场告诉我,这是残酷的, 所以我决定没有任何感觉, 切断他伤害我的能力。 这是一个愚蠢的誓言,一个没有孩子能完全保持的,但它给了我一种代理感或控制感. 两年之后,它得到了回报。
我九岁生日的主要礼物是篮球 当他决定我太喜欢它时 他用长刀刺它 但到那时,我已使自己变得足够坚固(再次成为机构),不感到悲伤,也不感到惊讶。 它是一个问题: 我哪来的钱买另一球? 我怎么保护它?
因为我可以判断我父亲的行为, 随着时间流逝,我和哥哥开始反抗他. 我们穿着厚厚的牛仔裤 当它看起来可能开始飞翔。 如果一击落地? 身体疼痛通常不会持续很长时间。 社会痛苦更严重。
家里人经常搬家,因为父亲总是可以找到工作,但过于不稳定,无法保留工作。 我在七年中就读了五所学校,主要在岛屿城镇。 我发现我的运动能力 让我通过一个或另一个团队交朋友。 除非男生需要数学冠军来抹去聪明女孩脸上的笑容,
我在想办法 直到家事变迁 也许是因为酒 也许是因为专业上的失败 父亲现在被降格为一个小乡村教会的监督,两个兼职工作,以及红十字会的暑期工作. 不管是什么原因 他的行为变得不祥
他日复一日地咒骂和愤怒,谴责他的敌人,激怒共产党员,激怒他的儿子们. 他继续打击我们,偶尔试图造成真正的伤害,当时我们12到15岁,但他也开始谈论杀死我们. 最后,他经常说,我们可以忽略它,直到我们听到他把他的枪从书架上刮下来。
当我们听到子弹响起时,当我们听到母亲喊着“跑!跑!”时,我们走了。 即使我们没有鞋子和外套, 即使冻雨泼了我们, 我们跑, 然后胡闹和颤抖 在桥下,试图猜测 他的愤怒何时会消散, 这样我们就可以冒险回到我们的房子。 唉,没有别的地方,没有朋友、家人或权威知道。 我們是獨自一人。
愤怒越来越频繁、更激烈, 我和哥哥意识到我们需要制定防御计划, 因为现在很清楚我们的母亲已经无法化解我们父亲的愤怒,
多年之后,我问她,“你认为他会在今后10分钟内杀死我们多少次?” 她搜寻她的记忆并叹息说:“四次。 也许5个。” 我们理解;我们必须自卫。 战略会议是超现实的,但至关重要。 备选案文1:逃跑。 如果我们在楼下, 我们会跑出一个门或跳 从某个窗口。
在楼上,我们有两个窗户没有锁,以防他挡住台阶。 其中一个引向了廊屋顶,一个七英尺或八英尺高的跳到后院;另一个则更高,但带着扭伤的脚踝逃跑比被困好. 备选案文2:动脉动。 我们打了很多棒球 在这个时候。
木头蝙蝠是常态,当它们破碎时,我们把它们分散在屋子里,总是保留一个靠近后门,一个放在前门,以防我们别无选择. 如果他陷害我们,我们中的一人必须攻击他,另一人必须获得一只球棒,用脚和膝盖狠狠地打他。
我知道,但不要说,我的哥哥,大而强壮,会攻击他,我会挥棒。 如果是死是生,我也许需要这样做。 请不要认为我主张用暴力对抗暴力。 我只是描述一个短期计划 不死。 我们的母亲应该打电话给当局。 我们也应该有。
不幸的是,我们当时无法看到这个选择。 不管是什么原因,我总是能从死亡威胁中解脱出来,这似乎是梦或者剧院. 不幸的是,父亲意识到他可以适应每个孩子的弱点。 身体的打击激怒了我的哥哥,所以父亲打了他的身体.
我弟弟很温柔 所以父亲用恶魔和黑暗力量来恐吓他 他选择用细微的侮辱来伤害我的精神,这些侮辱可以持续一天10,20,30分钟. 为什么? 因为我依靠某些技能找到朋友
他看见我的信心,于是想用一系列的话来摧毁它:“你无用,毫无价值,无助,你永远是。 你是弱者,就像新生的小猫, 盲目和无助, 低调地为牛奶。 是的,一只无助、无用、毫无价值的小猫。” 他看到, 于是他日复一日地重复了将近三年。
这些会议的规则是“你不能离开,也不能回答”。 所以我坐在椅子上听话 我怎么能反击? 谁能用棍子打坦克? 但我尽力了 我看着他,无动于衷, 与所有的不信任和蔑视 我的脸和姿势可能聚集。 然后,我列举了自己的技能,并在其中喊道:“我不是毫无价值的。
你错了。” 所以,我和我的兄弟们 试图,无论多么软弱, 为自己辩护。 虽然没有太多, 我们感到我们有一定程度的力量,这帮助了我们的生存。 我们感到我们有一定程度的力量,这帮助了我们的生存。 我们反抗的感觉 自我防卫 可能还击 导致我联手
author: Dan Doriani

title: Caring Well at Both Ends of Life (with Jen Wilkin)
summary: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor.
summary_zh: Melissa和Courtney和Jen Wilkin谈到,看到生命的开始和结束之间的相似之处,能帮助我们以同情和荣誉来照顾年老的亲人. 讨论我们文化如何优先注重自给自足, 他们分享照顾年老父母的故事, 资源参考:Jen Wilkin的《尘土变尘》,Whitney Pipkin的《Whitney Pipkin被Atul Gawande 相关资源:5种方式来纪念一个年老的爱人(即使是在困难的时候) 照顾老年父母照顾者受痴呆之苦的欢乐: 父亲和母亲讨论的问题: 1.
title_zh: 在生命的两个端点都给予关怀（与珍·威尔金）
content: Melissa and Courtney talk with Jen Wilkin about how seeing the parallels between the beginning of life and its end can help us care for aging loved ones with compassion and honor. They discuss how our culture’s prioritization of self-sufficiency poorly prepares us for the day when we’ll need to accept help. They share their stories of caring for aging parents and talk about how they’re seeking to number their own days aright as they age. Resources Mentioned: Dust to Dust by Jen Wilkin We Shall All Be Changed by Whitney Pipkin Being Mortal by Atul Gawande Related Resources: 5 Ways to Honor an Aging Loved One (Even When It’s Hard) The Joy of Caring for Aging Parents Caregivers Suffer from Dementia Too Honor Your Father and Mother Discussion Questions: 1. Have you ever cared for someone during a season of significant need, or have you received that care? How did the experience shape your understanding of dependence on others? 2. Why can it be difficult to receive help from others, even when we know we need it? What does our reluctance to depend on others reveal about us? 3. Our culture often measures a person’s worth by his or her productivity or abilities. How does the gospel challenge those assumptions, especially as we age? 4. When we think about the possibility of losing some of our independence and abilities as we age, what truths about God and our identity in Christ give us hope? 5. How can churches help ensure that older adults (especially those without children or nearby family) are known and cared for? 6. What practices or habits do you want to cultivate to help you age well, both physically and spiritually?

title: Lessons from Ezra on Leading a Story You Didn’t Start
summary: Ezra entered a story God had already begun. Ezra teaches leaders how to continue God’s work in the lives of his people.
summary_zh: 在以斯拉书中,以斯拉甚至直到第七章才出现. 这说明在书名被命名的人登场之前, 在书中的布道系列结束很久之后,这种观察一直留在我身边。 我越深思熟虑,就越能与我的领导经验相呼应。 Ezra不是一个领导手册;
title_zh: 从以斯拉身上学到的关于领导一个并非由你开启的故事的经验教训
content: In the book of Ezra, Ezra doesn’t even appear until chapter 7. That means more than half the book unfolds before the man for whom it’s named ever steps onto the scene. That observation stayed with me long after our sermon series in the book ended. The more I reflected on it, the more it resonated with my experience of leadership. Ezra isn’t a leadership manual; the book’s primary purpose is to highlight God’s sovereignty and his steadfast commitment to carrying out his redemptive purposes in and through his people. But if we pay attention to how God uses Ezra in his ministry context, there is a word here to those called to lead stories they didn’t start. Story Ezra Entered Long before Ezra arrives, the Jewish exiles hear about the possibility of homecoming through King Cyrus’s decree, fulfilling the Word of the Lord spoken through Jeremiah (chap. 1). Stirred by the Spirit, they leave the lives they had grown accustomed to and journey home to Jerusalem (chap. 2). The rebuilding of the temple in Jerusalem begins, and when its foundation is completed, the exiles’ pent-up emotions erupt into shouts of joy and sorrow that could barely be distinguished from one another (chap. 3). Unexpected opposition then halts the rebuilding (chap. 4), but through a series of providential circumstances, the work resumes, and the temple is finally completed after a long journey of uncertainty (chap. 5–6). This story is already filled with so many layers: stirring of the Spirit, risk, courage, failure, emotions, disappointment, uncertainty, sovereignty, grace. Every chapter seems to beg for more stories to be told. The point is simple yet profound: Before Ezra ever leads, God is already at work. A story is already underway. Ezra 1–6 isn’t an extended introduction, as though everything before chapter 7 were simply a prelude to Ezra’s ministry. Rather, in God’s timing, Ezra is brought into a story far larger than himself. The same is true for many leaders today who inherit a story they didn’t start. Every church carries memories of joy and sorrow, faithfulness and failure, growth and disappointment. Every congregation has a history that inevitably shapes its present. Wise leaders recognize that they aren’t beginning God’s work; they’re joining it. Story Ezra Continued What, then, can Ezra show us about leading a story we didn’t start? Here are four lessons. 1. Pray first. When King Artaxerxes commissions Ezra to guide and teach God’s people who have returned to Jerusalem, Ezra prepares to enter this story by calling those traveling with him to fast and pray. Rather than relying on military protection to get him safely to Jerusalem, he turns to trusting in God’s provision and protection (chap. 7–8). Notice how quickly Ezra turns to prayer. Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Do you have a habit of praying? Pause often and pray something even as simple as this: “Lord, go before me and help me join where you are and what you’re doing.” Prayer reminds us who is ultimately going before us to build up his people. 2. Expect heartbreak. In Ezra 9, after beginning his teaching ministry and seeking spiritual renewal among the people, Ezra learns that God’s people have fallen into serious covenant unfaithfulness. His response is surprising: He tears his garments, pulls out his hair, and falls before God. His first response isn’t outrage: Why is this happening now? I just started my new role! It’s not damage control: How bad is the situation, and what are my immediate action items? And it’s not blame shifting: This problem predates me. Thank God I’m not responsible for this! Prayer positions our minds and hearts to actively walk in the reality that the story ultimately doesn’t depend on us. Ezra’s instinctive and immediate response is grief. Many leaders enter into new churches and ministry contexts hoping to teach, mentor, cast new vision, and build something impressive and influential. We rarely anticipate how much ministry will involve disappointment, betrayal, conflict, and heartbreak. Yet these experiences are often where God forms true shepherds and leaders. Ezra embodies this truth. He enters the story of the people he’s been called to serve. Ezra shows us that faithful leaders aren’t those who avoid heartbreak. They’re those who allow heartbreak to deepen their love for God’s people. This may be one of the most challenging and humbling tasks of a leader entering an already begun story. After all, we are not hardwired to naturally embrace heartbreak, especially when adjusting to a new ministry context is already difficult enough. Grief allows us to move beyond managing people and begin loving them, especially when their wounds, failures, and heartbreaks become our own. 3. Listen well. As Ezra grieves, Shecaniah steps up to speak on behalf of the people, acknowledging the seriousness of their corporate sin normalized through repeated practices and compromises. Ezra listens. He receives Shecaniah’s challenge and finds the courage to rise from his state of grief and take the necessary next step (chap. 10). Leaders often enter new contexts feeling pressure to arrive with answers. Ezra shows another way. He creates space to receive a timely nudge from one of his lay leaders and allows it to shape his next steps. Every church contains stories, wounds, and concerns that leaders will never discover unless they cultivate the humility to listen carefully. Sometimes the most faithful thing a leader can do in a new context is to create space for people to speak honestly, and take their words seriously enough to discern what God may be saying through them. Listening helps us to lay down our assumed answers and develop instincts to discern how God is already at work in a story that began before us. 4. Lead with courage. After prayer, confession, and discernment, Ezra gets up from his place of grief and leads the people toward confronting their covenant unfaithfulness and pursuing costly repentance (chap. 10). The path forward is complicated and uncomfortable, but Ezra understands that leadership requires courageous decisions and actions. Listening is essential, but it’s not the end of faithful and effective leadership. People need to be heard, but they also need to be led. Leaders entering new settings often fear being perceived as either passive or domineering. Some of that tension is inevitable, especially in a season of transition. The goal, however, is to lead from a posture marked by both the humility to listen and the courage to act. Such leaders know they won’t lead perfectly, but they trust God to provide the wisdom, timing, and courage they need each step along the way. The responsibility of leading reminds us that God is with us not only as we discern what needs to be done, but also as we take the difficult next step in turning a new chapter in a story. Story Christ Stepped Into Perhaps you’re inheriting a church where people still carry wounds from a previous pastor. Perhaps you’re stepping into a ministry context where certain practices have become untouchable, even if no one remembers why. Perhaps you’ve been thrust into a role you never planned for or called to a place you never imagined laying down roots, or you’re discovering that the story you thought you were entering isn’t the one unfolding in front of you. Whatever story God has placed you in, you can trust that he was there before you arrived. Before Ezra entered the scene, God had already stirred Cyrus’s heart, preserved his own covenant people, provided what they needed to rebuild the temple, and sustained them through opposition. God didn’t begin being faithful because Ezra arrived; God sovereignly brought Ezra into the already existing story to demonstrate his faithful purposes. This pattern in Ezra gives us more than a model for leadership; it points us to the gift and the way of our ultimate leader and Savior, Jesus Christ. While Ezra

在以斯拉书中,以斯拉甚至直到第七章才出现. 这说明在书名被命名的人登场之前, 在书中的布道系列结束很久之后,这种观察一直留在我身边。 我越深思熟虑,就越能与我的领导经验相呼应。 Ezra不是一个领导手册;
该书的主要目的是强调上帝的主权,以及他坚定致力于在人民中和通过人民实现他的发号施令的目的。 但若我们关注上帝如何用以斯拉为本,
故事以斯拉早在以斯拉到达之前就已经进入,犹太流亡者听到通过赛勒斯国王的诏书归国的可能性,满足了耶利米所讲的耶利米之言(第1章). 受精神驱使,他们离开已习惯的生活,回到耶路撒冷(第2章)。
在耶路撒冷重建该寺开始,当其基础完成后,流亡者的倒闭情绪爆发成欢乐和悲伤的呼声,几乎无法区分开来(第3章)。 意外的反对者然后停止重建(第三章)
4),但通过一系列的天生环境,工程恢复,神庙在经历了漫长的不确定之旅后终于完工(第5-6章). 这个故事已经充满了这么多层: 激起精神,风险,勇气,失败,情绪,失望,不确定,主权,恩典. 每一章似乎都乞求更多的故事被讲述.
这一点简单而深刻:在以斯拉开始前,上帝已经在工作。 一个故事已经开始了 Ezra 1-6并不是一个扩展的导言, 相反,根据上帝的时机,以斯拉被带入一个比他自己大得多的故事中。 今天许多领导人也一样,
每个教堂都背负着快乐和悲伤,忠诚和失败,成长和失望的记忆. 每个会堂都有着无可避免地塑造其现在的历史. 明智的领袖们认识到他们并没有开始上帝的工作, 故事以斯拉续作 那么,以斯拉能给我们展示一个我们没有开始的故事吗? 现为四课. 1. 先祷.
当阿尔塔克瑟斯国王委托以斯拉来引导和教导已返回耶路撒冷的上帝的人们时,以斯拉准备通过召唤和他一起旅行的人斋戒和祈祷来进入这个故事. 他没有依靠军事保护把他安全带到耶路撒冷,而是转而信任上帝的供养和保护(第7-8章)。 注意以斯拉如何迅速转向祈祷.
祈祷让我们的心灵和心灵在现实中积极行走, 你有祈祷的习惯吗? “主啊,你到我前面来,帮助我加入你的位置,以及你在做什么。 ” 祈祷会提醒我们,谁最终要到我们面前去建设自己的人民。 2. 期待心碎。
在以斯拉九世,伊兹拉在开始他的教学部和在人民中寻求精神复兴之后,得知上帝的人民陷入了严重的不忠的契约之中. 他的反应令人惊讶:  He哭其衣,拔其发,伏于神前. 他的第一反应不是愤怒: 为什么现在发生这种事? 我刚刚开始我的新角色!
情况有多糟, 而不是责难的转变: 这个问题在我之前就存在过。 感谢上帝, 祈祷让我们的心灵和心灵在现实中积极行走, Ezra的本能和即时反应是悲伤.
许多领导人进入了新的教会和部委背景,希望传授、指导、塑造新的愿景,并创造令人印象深刻和有影响力的东西。 我们很少预料到这个部门会有多少人失望、背叛、冲突和伤心。 然而,这些经历常常是上帝形成真正的牧羊人和领袖的地方。 以斯拉体现了这个真理.
他进入了他被召为服务的人的故事。 以斯拉告诉我们,忠实的领导人不是那些避免心碎的人。 他们让心碎加深对上帝人民的爱。 这也许是一位领导人进入一个已经开始的故事中最具有挑战性和最艰难的任务之一。
毕竟,我们并非硬要自然地接受心碎,特别是当适应新的部委环境已经够困难的时候。 悲伤让我们超越管理人民,开始爱他们,特别是当他们的伤痛、失败和心碎成为我们自己的时候。 3. 仔细听好。
随着以斯拉的悲痛,谢卡尼娅开始代表人民发言,承认他们的企业罪恶的严重性,通过反复的做法和妥协而正常化. 以斯拉谛听. 他接受了谢卡尼亚的挑战,找到了勇气从悲痛中站起来,并采取必要的下一步(第十章). 领导人往往进入新的环境,感到压力,想得到答案。
以斯拉显示另一种方式。 他创造了空间来接受他一位非专业领导人及时的推动,并允许它塑造他的下一步. 每个教堂都包含一些故事、伤痕和关切,除非领导人培养谦卑,认真倾听,否则他们永远不会发现。
有时领导者在新的背景下能够做的最忠实的事情就是为人们创造开诚布公的空间,并认真对待他们的言辞,以辨别上帝通过他们可能说的话. 倾听帮助我们放下假设的答案,并发展直觉,以辨别上帝如何在开始于我们面前的故事中已经发挥作用。 4. 勇敢地领导。
在祷告、忏悔和辨别之后,以斯拉从他的悲痛地点站起来,带领人民面对他们的不忠的契约,追求代价高昂的悔改(第十章)。 前进的道路既复杂又不舒服,但以斯拉明白领导需要勇敢的决定和行动.
倾听是关键,但这不是忠诚和有效的领导结束。 人民需要倾听,但他们也需要领导。 进入新环境的领导人往往害怕被视为被动或任性。 其中一些紧张是不可避免的,特别是在过渡时期。
然而,目标是从谦逊的倾听和采取行动的勇气所表现的姿态中起带头作用。 他们相信上帝会提供智慧、时机和勇气,
领导责任提醒我们,上帝与我们同在,不仅因为我们知道需要做什么,而且因为我们采取了困难的下一步,在故事中翻开新的篇章。 或许你正在继承一座教堂,
或许你正步入某些做法不可触及的部委范畴, 或许你被推向了一个你从未计划过的角色, 或被召唤到一个你从未想象过的地方,
无论上帝给你写了什么故事 你都能相信他在你到来之前在场 在以斯拉进入现场之前,上帝已经激怒了赛勒斯的心,维护了自己的盟约人民,提供重建神庙所需的条件,并通过反对维持他们. 上帝并没有因为以斯拉的到来而变得忠诚;
上帝主权地将以斯拉带入已经存在的故事,以展示他的忠实目的. 以斯拉的这种模式给我们的不仅仅是领导模式;它向我们指出了我们最终领袖和救主耶稣基督的天赋和方式. 以斯拉时
author: Benjamin Bae

title: When Families Sit Together in Church: The Missional Opportunity
summary: The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity.
summary_zh: 我认识的大多数牧师都在研究一个共同的问题: 我们如何更好地为那些来到教堂,觉得每个人都有家庭团体,没有人真正欢迎的人服务? 在最近一篇文章中,戴夫·摩尔(Dave Moore)认为为了大委员会,你应该停止与家人坐在教堂里. 他写道,“教会是别人的”,并说,我们应该从部署执行任务的角度考虑我们的教会出席。 这篇文章出现在福音联盟的澳大利亚网站.
title_zh: 当家人一起坐在教堂里：宣教的机会
content: Most pastors I know are working on a common problem: How do we better serve the people who come to church and feel like everyone has a family group and no one is genuinely welcoming? In a recent article , Dave Moore argues that for the sake of the Great Commission, you should stop sitting with your family at church. He writes that “church is for others” and says we should think of our church attendance in terms of deployment for mission. The article appeared on The Gospel Coalition’s Australian site. TGC’s international coalitions have their own independent editorial teams. All agree to publish resources that align with TGC’s Foundation Documents , but individual writers , staff members , and Council members often disagree on matters that fall outside our Confessional Statement and Theological Vision for Ministry. In this case, I respectfully disagree with Moore. Any church committed to reaching lost people and including outsiders is asking themselves how to best address the problems of cliques and people not feeling like they belong. But when Moore says that “dividing ourselves for the sake of others is the most beautiful picture of Christian unity,” I believe he overstates his case. The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. More than that, to present family members worshiping together as an obstacle to love for others neglects the mission of the family and God’s call to parents. Acknowledging legitimate situations where families can’t or don’t sit together in church, as Christians, we don’t choose between our families or our mission. Building gospel-centered families is Great Commission ministry. Families as Mission God commands parents to teach his words and ways diligently to their children (Deut. 6:7). We’re called to train up our children in the way they should go (Prov. 22:6). The Bible places a priority on the family as a first-order love over against providing for others (1 Tim. 5:8). The Bible doesn’t command families to divide in worship as a picture of Christian unity. The primary responsibility for showing children “the way they should go” belongs to the parents, not the people of God in the abstract (Gen. 18:19). Parents set the tone for the worshipful commitment of a household (Josh. 24:15). Parents are the generation that proclaims the works of God to the next generation (Ps. 145:4). When Moore writes that “church is special spiritual-family time,” he neglects another reality: The primary disciple-making responsibility for children in those spiritual families is given to nuclear families—namely, mothers and fathers. Modeling worship for your children is ministry. It’s a blessing for your children to watch you week after week learning from God’s Word and participating in the life of the church. It’s good to make people feel welcome at church—and that includes children. To be entrusted with children is to be entrusted with the mission of God: the passing of God’s worship from one generation to the next. Families on Mission At the same time, it’s good to be intentional about those who come into the church without a family, without community, without certainty that anyone cares about them. That’s true for our approach to lone believers, and it’s true for our approach to the lost. So how can we address that problem without treating the family like an obstacle to engaging the isolated? 1. Loving families can be welcoming families. The best path forward for engaging people alone at church isn’t by neglecting an essential commitment—the family—but by leveraging the family as a unit for mission. It’s not “Sorry kids, someone else is more important.” Instead it’s “Hey kids, this is our new friend. She’s going to sit with us today.” My wife and I have worked to show our kids not that others come before them but that others come with us because we love to include people in our lives. As Jen Oshman says , “We will never sacrifice our family for the mission; but we will sacrifice as a family for the mission.” 2. Churches can empower all members. One of the mistakes we make in the church is thinking everyone should do everything. The beauty of the body of Christ is that different people are gifted in different ways for different ministries. What about the empty-nesters who have love to give and do so unhurriedly? Could widows or single men be especially suited to notice newcomers in the church and connect with them? They have much to offer the church as ministry-givers, not just ministry-receivers, and can extend gospel welcome to other never-married singles and widows. 3. Godly families model worship for unbelieving or new families. Children aren’t the only people watching in worship. Immature fathers learn to model worship for their family by watching godly men do the same. Mothers accommodating busy-twisty-shifty kids can show mothers not used to getting their kids through a lengthy worship service how to do the same. Kids who have learned reverence and worship from godly parents can model it for the kids of families who are newer to church or whose children are younger. A lot of families that show up at churches don’t know how to be worshipers or how to be a family. When godly mothers and fathers model worship, they’re not just modeling it for their own kids. They’re modeling it for other families. 4. Godly families aren’t just committed to the gospel. They display it. Jesus hasn’t just affirmed marriage. He created it and endowed it with a sacred purpose: to be a picture of the gospel itself. It’s no small thing that godly marriages embody the profound mystery of the gospel (Eph. 5:32). When families worship together, led by husbands and wives confessing their shared loved for Jesus, we communicate to onlookers the love of the gospel itself. When parents lovingly respond to wriggling kids, we show outsiders how they too can be met with kindness, even if they’re a bit of a mess. When godly mothers and fathers model worship, they’re not just modeling it for their own kids. They’re modeling it for other families. It’s not just good for husbands and wives to sit together—it can be good for them to hold hands, to lean on each other, to pray with heads close together. This “ holy estate ” isn’t just a matter of social convenience. It’s a “mystical union” that tells the world about Christ’s love for his church. For those of us blessed with children, we’ve been called to an important stewardship. Yes, in the freedom of Christ, we may occasionally “divide and conquer.” Pastors and worship volunteers regularly sit apart from their families in the sanctuary. Families on the mission field may be separated on Sundays for a season. In my own family, my wife recently stepped away in worship to embrace a grieving woman in our congregation. But most Sundays you’ll find us together, usually on the right side of the sanctuary, with our kids. Don’t mistake that placement for convenience. Under the surface, you’ll find commitment: to teach our children by our words and deeds to know and worship God. And if you look close enough, or go to the Mexican restaurant in town after church, you’ll often notice we have a guest or a single person with us. Our table always includes four—but it also always has room for more.
content_zh:
我认识的大多数牧师都在研究一个共同的问题: 我们如何更好地为那些来到教堂,觉得每个人都有家庭团体,没有人真正欢迎的人服务? 在最近一篇文章中,戴夫·摩尔(Dave Moore)认为为了大委员会,你应该停止与家人坐在教堂里.
他写道,“教会是别人的”,并说,我们应该从部署执行任务的角度考虑我们的教会出席。 这篇文章出现在福音联盟的澳大利亚网站. TGC的国际联盟有自己的独立编辑团队.
所有人都同意发布与TGC基金会文件一致的资源,但个人作家、工作人员和理事会成员往往对不属于我们的《忏悔声明》和《对部委的神学展望》的事项持不同意见。 在这种情况下,我恭敬地不同意摩尔。
任何致力于接触失去的人和包括外来者在内的教会,都问自己如何最好地解决那些认为不属于他们的集团和人民的问题。 但是,当摩尔说“为了他人而分裂我们是基督教团结的最美丽的图景”时,我认为他夸大了他的案情。
《圣经》并没有命令家庭在礼拜中分裂, 更何况,让家庭成员一起礼拜成为爱他人的障碍,忽视了家庭的使命和上帝对父母的召唤.
承认家庭不能或不能坐在教堂里的合法情况, 建筑福音家庭是大委员会部。 家庭作为使命之神,命令父母向子女勤勉地传授他的言辞和方法(德国6:7)。
我们被要求以他们应该走的路来训练我们的孩子(Prov. 22:6)。 《圣经》把家庭放在优先地位,作为反对供养他人的第一流的爱情(1 Tim.5:8)。 《圣经》并没有命令家庭在礼拜中分裂,
向儿童展示“他们应该走的路”的主要责任在于父母,而不是抽象的上帝的人民(Gen.18:19)。 父母为一个家庭的虔诚承诺定下了基调(Josh. 24:15). 父母是向下一代宣示神功的一代(P145:4).
当摩尔写道“教堂是特殊的精神家庭时间”, 这些精神家庭中儿童的主要门徒责任赋予核心家庭,即父母。 为孩子做模特是部里的事
周而复始地看着你学习上帝的话, 让人们在教堂感到受欢迎, 托付给孩子就是托付给上帝的使命:上帝的崇拜从一代传到下一代.
出差家属 同时,对于那些没有家庭、没有社区、没有确定任何人关心他们的人来说,这是有意的。 我们对待孤独的信徒的做法也是如此, 因此,我们如何在不把家庭当作孤立者接触的障碍的情况下解决这个问题? 一、导 言
喜爱的家庭可以是欢迎家庭. 让人们单独参与教会的最佳途径不是忽视一项基本承诺, 不是“对不起, 这是我们的新朋友。
她今天要和我们坐在一起。 我的妻子和我努力向我们的孩子表明,不是别人在他们面前,而是其他人与我们一起来,因为我们喜欢把人纳入我们的生活。 正如Jen Oshman所说,“我们永远不会为使命牺牲我们的家人;但我们将为使命牺牲我们的家庭。” 2. 教会可以赋予所有成员权力。
我们教会的错误之一是认为每个人都应该做任何事情. 基督身体的美丽之处在于不同的人以不同的方式为不同的部会所天赋. 空亡之徒,有爱而无急,此何也? 寡妇或单身男子是否特别适合在教堂里发现新来的人并与他们联系?
他们可以向教会提供很多作为牧师的礼物,而不仅仅是牧师的接收者,并且可以向其他从未结婚的单身者和寡妇提供福音的欢迎。 3. 神户模式崇拜不可信或新家庭。 儿童并不是唯一在礼拜中观看的人。 不成熟的父亲通过观察神明的男子也这样做来学习为家人树立崇拜的模范.
照顾忙碌的潮流儿童的母亲可以向母亲展示,她们不习惯通过长时间的礼拜服务来让孩子如何做同样的事情。 从神灵父母那里学到尊敬和崇拜的孩子们,可以为那些年纪较新到教堂或子女年龄较小的家庭的孩子树立榜样.
许多在教堂露面的家庭都不知道如何做礼拜者, 他们不只是为自己的孩子做模特。 他们为其他家庭做模特。 4. 神明的家庭不仅仅致力于福音。 他们展示它。 耶稣不只是确认婚姻。
他创造了它,并赋予它一个神圣的目的:成为福音本身的照片. 这并非一件小事, 当家庭在丈夫和妻子的带领下一起礼拜,承认他们共同爱耶稣时,我们向旁观者传达福音本身的爱。
当父母热情地回应孩子们时, 我们向外人展示, 他们不只是为自己的孩子做模特。 他们为其他家庭树立榜样。
丈夫和妻子坐在一起并不只是好事, 这“圣地”不仅仅是社会方便的问题。 向全世界讲述基督对教会的热爱。 对我们这些有孩子的人来说,
是的,在基督的自由中,我们偶尔会“分裂和征服”。 牧师和崇拜志愿者经常在圣所与家人分开坐。 任务现场的家属可以在星期天分居一个季节. 在我自己的家庭中,我妻子最近为了在我们的会众中拥抱一个悲痛的女人而走开。
但大部分星期天你会发现我们在一起, 不要为了方便而误解这个位置。 在表面上,你会找到承诺:用我们的言行教导我们的孩子了解和崇拜上帝。
如果你看起来足够近, 或者在教堂后去墨西哥餐厅, 我们的餐桌总是包括四个——但它也总是有更大的空间。
author: Griffin Gulledge

title: Beyond the Battlefield: Veteran Suicide and the Value of Life
summary: On Veterans Day, we celebrate the willingness of those who have served and are serving to sacrifice for our country.
summary_zh: 「我们会教你如何杀人。 当你回来时,你就是退伍军人协会的问题。 他们告诉我的老中士, 杀害或被杀的风险是兵役不可回避的一部分。 在军队中,新兵在基本战斗训练中经历了一个编队过程,使他们变成了士兵.
title_zh: 战场之外：退伍军人自杀与生命的价值
content: “We’ll teach you how to kill. When you get back, you’re the VA’s problem.” That’s what they told my old team sergeant before he deployed to Afghanistan with the 82nd Airborne Division. The risk of killing or being killed is an inescapable part of military service. In the Army, recruits go through a formation process in Basic Combat Training that turns them into soldiers. Part of this means learning that the mission always comes first, which in turn must mean they’re expendable. First aid is taught with the assumption that at some point, someone will need a tourniquet, chest seal, or body bag. After all, the enemy also learns to shoot, and sometimes the mission requires soldiers to get into harm’s way. That’s part of the tragic necessity of war. No one would have followed Washington across the Delaware or left the landing craft on D-Day if staying alive were the number-one goal. A commander’s ability to orchestrate force in combat would break down with a military unwilling to die. But this same dynamic that makes militaries potent threatens the lives of those who fight, through the tragedy of veteran suicide. Necessity of Sacrifice We must understand sacrifice as more than mere operational necessity: Something is lost when nothing is worth dying for. C. S. Lewis famously warned of the danger of making men without chests—of a people without an anchoring morality to mediate the carnal passions of the stomach and the cold calculations of the head. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character, to say nothing of its national defense. Americans ought to be thankful that thousands of young men and women regularly sign the dotted line to join the armed forces, volunteering to put their country’s well-being ahead of their own. A society full of people consumed with their own survival doesn’t bode well for its moral character. The willingness to sacrifice that makes a military effective can carry a hidden cost. What happens when a soldier learns to put his life second, then struggles to understand its value when the mission ends? A soldier who was prepared to take a bullet downrange may think little of a bottle of whiskey, a pack of cigarettes, or opening up his motorcycle on the highway. When the Mission Ends Those who make it back from combat alive aren’t entirely safe. Veterans take their own lives at roughly twice the rate of the general population. Veteran suicide stems from a number of factors, including post-traumatic stress, moral injury, difficulty transitioning to civilian life, loss of purpose and social connection, traumatic brain injury, pain, and proximity to firearms. Alongside these factors, we should consider what it means to spend years learning to put one’s life second and what happens when that lesson outlasts the mission. There’s an obvious tension when it comes to the value of life. Christians know that our lives in this world aren’t ultimate (Rev. 12:11). Christians can face death because we recognize this life’s limits, while still treating life as a gift worthy of protection. As Jesus taught, being willing to die for others is the highest form of love (John 15:13). This is why the second person of the Trinity stepped down from heaven, took on the form of a servant, and obediently followed the Father’s mission orders to death on the cross (Phil. 2:6–8). Yet Jesus didn’t throw his life away; he demonstrated perfect courage. Between the foolhardiness that leads to blood on the highway and the cowardice that keeps men in hiding when a wolf growls at the door, stands courage. As G. K. Chesterton observes, “Courage is almost a contradiction in terms. It means a strong desire to live taking the form of a readiness to die.” We see this in Christ’s agony in anticipation of the cross in the garden of Gethsemane (Luke 22:44). Yet he carried his cross anyway. Value of Life and Virtue of Sacrifice The Christian worldview ties together the value of both life and sacrifice, offering hope for the coward and the reckless alike. That’s the power of the gospel. Humans are made in the image of God, filled with inherent value (Gen. 1:27). Our bodies are temples that were bought at a price (1 Cor. 6:19–20). Though we sinners fail to bear God’s image faithfully, Jesus loved us enough to die on the cross for our sins (Rom. 5:8). He dignifies us by giving us the mission of serving as ambassadors of heaven in this life (2 Cor. 5:20). That mission sometimes requires sacrifice. Christians can face death because we recognize this life’s limits, while still treating life as a gift worthy of protection. On Veterans Day, we celebrate the willingness of those who have served and are serving to sacrifice for our country. In some ways, their willingness to sacrifice mirrors Christ’s sacrificial love. We can also remind veterans that their lives matter. The gospel gives us hope that our existence continues to matter when our work on earth is done. The mission may have ended, but their value has not. With the hope of the new creation ahead, Christians are free to love our lives and our bodies while still being willing to sacrifice both for others. We know that the ultimate reward isn’t self-preservation in this life but union with God in the new heavens and new earth. That’s good news for all of us, and it may be just the news a veteran needs to hear today.
content_zh:
「我们会教你如何杀人。 当你回来时,你就是退伍军人协会的问题。 他们告诉我的老中士, 杀害或被杀的风险是兵役不可回避的一部分。 在军队中,新兵在基本战斗训练中经历了一个编队过程,使他们变成了士兵.
这其中一部分意味着要了解特派团总是第一,这反过来必然意味着特派团是消耗性的。 急救的教学假设是,在某个时候,某人需要止血带,胸章,或身体袋. 毕竟,敌人也学会射击,有时任务需要士兵进入伤害的道路. 这是战争的悲惨必要性的一部分。
没有人会跟随华盛顿穿越特拉华州 或离开登陆艇 在D -Day,如果活着是头号进球。 指挥官在战斗中协调武力的能力会随着不愿牺牲的军方而瓦解. 但是,使军队强大起来的这种动态,通过老兵自杀的悲剧,威胁到那些战斗者的生命。
牺牲的必要性 我们必须把牺牲理解为不仅仅是行动上的必要:当没有什么值得牺牲时,就失去了某些东西。 C.S.Lewis有名地警告说,使没有胸怀的人——一个没有扎根道德的民族——去调解胃部的性欲和头部的冷淡计算有危险。
一个充满自生自灭的人的社会, 美国人应该感谢成千上万的年轻男女定期签署加入武装部队的标语,自愿将国家福祉置于自己首位。
一个充满了自身生存的人的社会, 使军事效力的牺牲意愿可能带来隐蔽的代价。 当一个士兵学会了把生命放在第二位,然后在任务结束时挣扎着去理解它的价值时,会发生什么?
一个准备拿子弹下游的士兵可能会想一瓶威士忌,一包香烟,或者在高速公路上打开他的摩托车. 当任务结束时, 退伍军人自杀率约为一般人口的两倍。
退伍军人自杀源于若干因素,包括创伤后压力、精神伤害、向平民生活过渡的困难、目的和社会联系的丧失、创伤性脑损伤、痛苦和接近火器。 除了这些因素之外,我们应该考虑用多年时间学习如何将一个人的生命置于第二位,以及这一教训超过任务时会发生什么。
在生命价值方面, 基督徒知道,我们在这个世界上的生活并非是终极的(Rev.12:11)。 基督徒可以面对死亡,因为我们认识到生命的极限,同时仍将生命视为值得保护的礼物。 正如耶稣所教导的,愿意为他人而死是爱的最高形式(John 15:13).
正因为如此,三位一体的第二人从天而降,采取仆人的形式,服从父亲的使命,在十字架上死亡(Phil. 2:6-8). 但耶稣并没有放弃他的生命;他表现出完美的勇气。
在导致高速公路上流血的愚蠢和怯懦之间,当狼咆哮在门前时,人们会躲藏起来,勇敢地站着. 正如G.K.Chesterton所指出,“勇气几乎是一种矛盾。 这意味着强烈希望以准备死亡的形式生活。” 我们从基督的痛苦中看到这一点,
但他还是带着十字架 牺牲生命和道德的价值 基督教的世界观将生命和牺牲的价值联系在一起,为懦夫和鲁莽者提供了希望。 这就是福音的力量。 人类以上帝的形象造就,充满固有价值(1:27). 我们的尸体是被价钱购买的寺庙(1 Cor 6:19-20).
虽然我们罪人没有忠实地承受上帝的形象,但耶稣却十分爱我们,为我们的罪行而死在十字架上(5:8). 他授予我们这个生命中担任天堂大使的任务(第5:20条),使我们深受尊重。 这项任务有时需要牺牲。 基督徒可以面对死亡,因为我们认识到生命的极限,同时仍将生命视为值得保护的礼物。
在退伍军人日,我们庆祝那些曾经和正在为我国献身的人的意愿。 在某些方面,他们牺牲的意愿反映了基督的牺牲爱。 我们还可以提醒退伍军人,他们的生命很重要。 福音给我们带来了希望,即当我们在地球上的工作完成时,我们的生存仍然重要。 任务可能已经结束,但其价值没有。
带着未来新创造的希望,基督徒可以自由地热爱我们的生活和身体,同时仍然愿意为他人牺牲两者. 我们知道,最终的回报并不是在今世的自我保护,而是在新天地中与上帝联合。 这对我们所有人来说都是好消息,
author: Tommy Doles

title: How We Saw God’s Goodness Through Our Child’s Cancer
summary: It was not in the good moments where God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive.
summary_zh: 面对深刻的痛苦就是与孤立相搏。 从乔布在灰烬中的座位到邻居的损失, 我们家族的癌症旅程就是这样。 我们感到孤独。 我们感到与那些听到消息的人断绝关系,甚至是无助的。
title_zh: 我们如何通过孩子的癌症看到神的良善
content: To encounter profound suffering is to wrestle with isolation. From Job’s seat in the ashes to your neighbor’s loss, news of suffering often includes a struggle to connect. Our family’s cancer journey was like that. We felt alone. And we sensed disconnection—even helplessness—from people who heard the news. Childhood cancer is a blessedly uncommon experience, but navigating pain is inherent to life in a fallen world. When we encounter others’ pain, we have a “Good Samaritan choice”—to step forward and show compassion or to walk away. Nightmare Our 3-year-old son, Ben, had an unexplained illness. After a week in the hospital, we were ushered into an ICU conference room full of doctors and nurses. They delivered the news: “Your son has cancer.” One of the nurses was crying before they even said a word. Our family is from Washington, DC, but we were about 10,000 miles from home. We’d been serving as missionaries in Costa Rica, yet we weren’t there either. On that January day, we were in a hospital in Sydney, Australia, on our dream trip—a family Christmas in summertime. It was quickly becoming a nightmare. The days after the diagnosis were filled with rapid changes. We couldn’t go back to Costa Rica. Returning to DC was almost impossible. The Ronald McDonald House was our new home. My daughter started kindergarten at a new school, in a new country. She drew a picture of her family. There was no home, garden, or pets—just a hospital bed. Ben on his last day of chemotherapy / Courtesy of Peter Morris Over the next six months, Ben endured 96 nights in the hospital, 25 general anesthetics, and chemotherapy so strong it could blind or even kill an adult. He was traveling through the metaphorical valley of the shadow of death, and it was decorated with bright colors and superhero stickers. May 22 is a day we still celebrate in our family as “no more chemo day.” Ben took his final dose of chemotherapy, and we rejoiced with a trip to McDonald’s and a chocolate cake. Despite the celebration, the years ahead held mortal peril. His doctor told us relapse was a risk without a treatment plan. All we could do was watch and wait. Ben was immunocompromised for the years that followed, extending into the 2020s when the disruption of a health crisis—previously rare—became globally mundane. Today, Ben’s body still carries the scars of his cancer and the side effects of the lifesaving treatment he received. But he’s a survivor. To any passerby, he looks like an ordinary 12-year-old boy. My wife and I have scars too. But we also carry the lessons the Lord taught us along the way. Those lessons are available to all believers as we encounter the pain of others. Here are three that stand out. 1. You can’t depend on people. Suffering has an odd way of resetting relationships. We saw it repeatedly, in our experience and with other cancer families we met. The apparent uniqueness of the suffering—and the emotional reactions it stirred—drove some people away. They wouldn’t, or couldn’t, step close and walk with us. However, those people stepping away opened the door to gospel opportunities for us. Australian hospitals rarely have private rooms, so we spent most of our 96 nights sharing rooms with people from diverse cultures and faiths. As other people pulled back from them, we were able to step forward and hold out the hope of the gospel in a dark and hopeless place. 2. You can depend on people. While some in our life pulled away, others chose to pull close. We were thousands of miles from our church family, but people still found ways to care for us. When we shared the news about Ben’s illness, our Facebook post reached more than 15,000 people around the world. It wasn’t the eyeballs that made a difference but the thoughtful actions. Local believers jumped into action with a meal roster. Costa Rican friends translated our English updates to equip our Spanish-speaking friends to pray. American friends prepared care packages, sent encouraging texts, and came to visit. For every person who had pulled away, we were blessed by more who pulled close with gestures—large and small—to encourage and support us. 3. God will use suffering to demonstrate his sovereign care. John Piper memorably said that “God is always doing 10,000 things in your life, and you may be aware of three of them.” From the oncology ward, it felt like our awareness grew to 10! There was a late-night delivery of goldfish crackers, the miraculous provision of a cheese pizza, and countless answers to prayer as the treatment progressed. For every person who had pulled away, we were blessed by more who pulled close. But it wasn’t in the good moments when God’s care was most evident. It was in the dark moments, often at night, when we were unsure if our son would survive. Feeling isolated and alone, we stared around the cold hospital room—and God showed up, again and again. He comforted our hearts, he led us to passages in his Word, and he provided text messages of encouragement at just the right time. We’re deeply thankful that the Lord spared our boy, but his goodness was most evident when we didn’t know if he would. Hope for Next Time Courtesy of Peter Morris When you look beneath the surface of our unique journey with cancer, you see a universal human journey through pain and uncertainty. We can all learn a lesson here. When you see people in your life encountering “unique” suffering, don’t pull away. Instead, pull close. Ask how you can pray for them. Text them with a verse. Bring a meal. Keep showing up. As you look for practical ways to serve, bring eyes looking for God’s sovereign care. Whether the news is good or bad, you’ll find him working there.
content_zh:
面对深刻的痛苦就是与孤立相搏。 从乔布在灰烬中的座位到邻居的损失, 我们家族的癌症旅程就是这样。 我们感到孤独。 我们感到与那些听到消息的人断绝关系,甚至是无助的。
童年时期的癌症是一种吉祥的罕见经历,但航海痛苦是堕落世界中生命所固有的. 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,我们有一个“好撒玛利亚人的选择”——站出来表示同情或离开。 噩梦我们3岁的儿子,本,有一个无法解释的疾病。 在医院里呆了一个星期后,我们被带入了一个由医生和护士组成的ICU会议室.
他们播下了一个消息:“你的儿子得了癌症。 其中一个护士甚至还没说一句话就哭了. 我们的家庭来自华盛顿特区 但我们离家约一万英里 我们一直担任哥斯达黎加的传教士, 1月当天,我们在澳大利亚悉尼的一家医院进行梦想之旅——夏天是家庭圣诞节。
它很快变成了一场噩梦。 诊断后的几天充满了快速的变化. 我们无法回到哥斯达黎加。 返回华盛顿几乎是不可能的。 罗纳德麦当劳之家是我们的新家 我女儿在新学校开始上幼儿园, 在新国家。 她画了一张她家人的照片。 没有家,没有花园,也没有宠物,只有一张医院床。
本最后一天的化疗 / 彼得・莫里斯的礼仪 在接下来的六个月里,本在医院忍受了96个晚上,25个一般麻醉药,化疗如此强大,可以盲目甚至杀死成人. 他穿梭在死亡阴影的隐喻山谷中,装饰着明亮的颜色和超级英雄贴纸.
5月22日仍是我们家庭庆祝的一天, Ben接受了最后的化疗, 尽管有庆典, 未来的岁月仍然有致命的危险。 他的医生告诉我们 复发是一种风险 没有治疗计划。 我们能做的就是观察和等待。
其后的几年里,本被免疫妥协,一直延续到2020年代,以前罕见的一次健康危机的破坏成为全球风云。 今天,Ben的身体仍带有癌症的伤疤和他接受救生治疗的副作用。 但他是个幸存者。 对于任何路人来说,他看起来像一个普通的12岁男孩. 我妻子和我也有伤疤
但我们也带着上帝教给我们的教训 当我们遇到其他人的痛苦时,所有信徒都可以接受这些教训。 这是三个突出的。 1. 你不能依赖人。 受苦有怪异的重构关系方式. 我们从我们的经验和我们遇到的其他癌症家庭中反复看到。
痛苦的明显独特性——以及它激起的情绪反应——驱赶一些人。 他们不会或无法靠近我们, 然而,那些走开的人为我们带来了机会。 澳大利亚的医院很少有私人房间,因此我们在96个晚上的大部分时间都与来自不同文化和信仰的人共用房间.
当其他人从他们那里撤退时,我们得以挺身而出,在一个黑暗和无望的地方抓住福音的希望。 2. 你可以依赖人。 在我们生命中有些人被拉走时,另一些人选择拉近。 我们离教会家数千英里 但人们仍然想方设法照顾我们
当我们分享本病的消息时, 并不是眼球的作用, 当地信徒以餐具名册跳跃行动. 哥斯达黎加朋友翻译了英语最新消息,
美国朋友准备了护理包,发了鼓舞人心的短信,并前来拜访. 对于每一个已经撤离的人来说,我们得到更多的人祝福,他们以大小的姿态拉近,鼓励和支持我们。 3. 上帝将利用苦难来表明其主权关怀。
约翰·皮珀回忆道,“上帝在你的生活中总是做一万件事情,你可能知道其中三件事情。” 从肿瘤病房,它感觉我们的意识 增长到10! 晚间送来金鱼饼干 神奇的奶酪披萨 和无数的祈祷答案 随着治疗的进展
对于每一个已经退出的人来说, 我们得到了更多的谁拉近。 但并不是在上帝的关心最明显的时候。 那是在黑暗的时刻,常常是晚上, 当我们不确定我们的儿子会生存。 我们感到孤立和孤独,在寒冷的医院房间周围凝视——上帝一次又一次地出现。
他安慰了我们的心,他带领我们读到了他的话中的段落,他在恰到好处的时候提供了鼓励的短信. 但我们不知道他是否愿意,
Peter Morris的下一时节的希望 当你看着我们独特的癌症之旅的表面之下, 你会看到人类通过痛苦和不确定而经历的普世旅程。 我们在这里都能吸取教训。 当人们在生活中遇到“独特的”苦难时, 相反,拉近。 问如何是祖师西来意. 用诗句给他们发短信。 带饭来. 继续出现.

title: On Christmas, God Shook Up the World
summary: Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants.
summary_zh: 读之曰:万军之 耶和華如此说:然而,不久,我必震动天地,海旱之地. 我将震动所有国家,使所有国家的宝藏都进来,我将以荣耀填满这个房子,这是宿主之 耶和華所说的. (汉语). 2:6-7) 反射 当这个预言在公元前520年来到哈加伊时,有谁想到上帝会与伯利恒谦卑父母所生的孩子一起震撼世界?
title_zh: 在圣诞节，上帝震撼了世界
content: Read For thus says the LORD of hosts: Yet once more, in a little while, I will shake the heavens and the earth and the sea and the dry land. And I will shake all nations, so that the treasures of all nations shall come in, and I will fill this house with glory, says the LORD of hosts. (Hag. 2:6–7) Reflect When this prophecy came to Haggai in 520 BC, did anyone imagine that God would shake up the world with a baby born to humble parents in Bethlehem? Or that “a little while” would be more than 500 years later? Yet if Advent teaches us anything, it’s that the Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. His timeline may not align with ours, but in the passage of centuries we experience his mercy. We read in 2 Peter 3:9, “The Lord is not slow to fulfill his promise as some count slowness, but is patient toward you, not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance.” The Lord works according to his own schedule and doesn’t act as we expect. In Hebrews 12:26, the writer expands on this relationship between patience and judgment by quoting Haggai 2. The shaking is a kind of sifting, like the sand separated from jewels in a strainer. The Lord shakes the world to sift out anyone who doesn’t worship that baby born in Bethlehem. Because even as a helpless babe, he is the King of kings and Lord of lords who will reign forever. In Jesus we see “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” the One who “upholds the universe by the word of his power” (Heb. 1:3). One day, after a little while, that baby would grow up and exercise his power in the most unexpected way. He would submit to death, even on a cross. The day he died on Calvary, the temple curtain was torn in two. An earthquake shook the city. Rocks split at the Place of a Skull (Matt. 27:32, 51). That helpless man, bloodied and beaten, commanded more authority than anyone else had realized—including the power to judge his judges. The Roman officer who commanded 100 confessed, “Truly this was the Son of God!” (v. 54). Those who don’t follow suit will be sifted. But the shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. By this sacrifice, believers will receive a “kingdom that cannot be shaken” (Heb. 12:28). To this kingdom all the treasures of the nations will accrue, as Haggai foresaw with the temple filled by God’s glory. God did this for the Hebrews when he delivered them from slavery. They plundered the Egyptians (Ex. 12:36). And he’ll do it again when he delivers the world from death, as the kings of the earth bring their glory to the temple in the new Jerusalem (Rev. 21:24). The shed blood of the only Son of God has the power to forgive the sins of all who repent. These kings will follow a path already trod by the wise men of the east, who tracked the star to baby Jesus. From the nations they brought their treasures—gold, frankincense, and myrrh. The purported king, Herod, could only see a threat. But these wise men fell down and worshiped the baby still nursing with his mother, Mary (Matt. 2:11). Do you see the power and the glory concealed from the world while contained in that baby? Do you see in him a King whose love for sinners kept him nailed to the cross? Advent is waiting for something that not everyone can see. Advent is preparing to receive a gift that not everyone wants. Advent is enduring an unstable world with hope because an unshakable kingdom is coming—in a little while. Respond How might the Lord’s seeming lack of action express his patience for you? How could you help your non-Christian friends and family see the glory in Jesus this Advent season?

2:6-7) 反射 当这个预言在公元前520年来到哈加伊时,有谁想到上帝会与伯利恒谦卑父母所生的孩子一起震撼世界? 或者说,“一小段时间”将会是500多年之后? 但是如果Advent教我们什么, 那就是上帝按照自己的计划工作,
他的时间可能与我们的时间不符,但在几个世纪的过去中,我们感受到了他的怜悯。 我们在2 Peter 3:9中读到,“上帝不迟缓地履行他的承诺,因为他有些迟缓,但对你们是忍耐的,不希望任何人灭亡,但愿所有人都悔过自新。” 主按照自己的计划工作,
在希伯来语12:26中,作家通过引用哈盖2(英语:Haggai 2. 摇晃是一种筛法,如在教练器中从珠宝中分离出来的沙子. 主震撼世界,以筛除任何不崇拜伯利恒出生的婴儿的人。 因为即使作为一个无助的宝贝,他是国王的国王和将永远统治的领主.
在耶稣中,我们看到“上帝荣耀的光芒及其本性的确切印记”,即“以其力量之言维持宇宙者”(Heb.1:3)。 有一天,过了一阵子,这个孩子会成长,并以最意想不到的方式行使他的力量. 他会屈从于死地 即使是在十字架上 在卡尔瓦里逝世的那天,神庙的幕帘被撕成两半.
地震震撼了整个城市. 石头在一个骷髅的地方分裂(Matt. 27:32,51). 这个无助的、血淋淋的、被殴打的人,比任何其他人所意识到的都掌握了更大的权威,包括审判其法官的权力。 指挥100人的罗马军官承认,“这确是天子!” (v. 54)。 不跟随的人会被筛杀。
惟天子之流血,则能饶恕一切悔罪之罪. 通过这一牺牲,信徒将获得“无法动摇的王国”(Heb:12:28)。 国家所有珍贵的财宝都会到这王国来, 上帝为希伯来人这样做 当他把他们从奴隶中解救出来。
他们掠夺埃及人(Ex. 12:36). 将世界从死亡中拯救出来, 惟天子之流血,能饶罪于忏悔者. 这些国王将沿着一条已经由东方的智者所踏过的路,他们追随星辰来婴儿耶稣.
他们从国中拿来他们的财宝--金的、坦率的、 myrrh。 自称的国王希律只能看见威胁 但是这些智者倒下了,并崇拜着婴儿仍然和母亲玛丽一起哺乳(Matt2:11). 你看见那个孩子身上 隐藏着力量和荣耀吗? 你看见他有一个国王吗? 他爱的罪人把他钉在十字架上?
基督在等待着别人看不到的东西 基督正在准备接受 不是每个人都想要的礼物。 基督正在充满希望地忍受一个不稳定的世界,因为一个不可动摇的王国即将来临。 响应 主看来缺乏行动,
你怎能帮助你的非基督教朋友和家人看到耶稣的荣耀?
author: Collin Hansen

title: Midlife Is a Crossroads, Not a Crisis
summary: In ‘Good News for Midlife,’ Jared Wilson reminds us to embrace our midlife crossroads, find new meaning in service to others, and let this season be an opportunity to discover grace upon grace in Jesus.
summary_zh: 去年,我和一位二十多岁的学生坐在教堂里 他说他正在寻找一个年长的人来指导他,我开始通过我们的神明,智慧的人在50到60岁的时候思考. 他阻止了我,并澄清说: 他让我指导他 “等等,你以为我老了吗? ” 我今年42岁, 有人大声问起我生下来是不是老了 我承认这个新奇的季节促使我去寻找智慧。
title_zh: 中年是一个十字路口，而不是危机
content: Last year, I was sitting with an early twentysomething grad student in our church. He said he was looking for an older man to mentor him, and I started thinking through our godly, wise men in their 50s and 60s. He stopped me and clarified: He was asking me to mentor him. “Wait, you think I’m old?!” I’m 42, and to be fair, I’ve been told I’m an “old soul” my whole life. Some have wondered aloud if I was born old. While I still don’t feel old, I’ll admit this new and strange season has spurred me to go looking for wisdom. I’ll tell you, reading about midlife is depressing. According to studies, happiness in life follows a U-shaped curve. Our self-reported happiness starts high in childhood, then decreases into adolescence and further into early adulthood. It bottoms out somewhere around age 46—smack in the center of middle age—before beginning to rise again and steadily increasing into our twilight years. Further, studies have shown that depression and anxiety also are highest around the age of 45. Despite all the bad news, Good News for Midlife: Navigating Middle Age with Guts and Grace was encouraging. Writing from his early 50s, Jared Wilson, associate professor of pastoral ministry at Midwestern Baptist Theological Seminary, understands the challenges of midlife but also provides refreshing hope for those of us finding our own way through. Understand Midlife Most definitions place “middle age” as 40 to 60, but it’s probably more accurate to describe midlife in terms of its demands and responsibilities. For me, it looks something like this: I still feel energetic, but it takes far longer to recover from lost sleep, injuries, and travel. My kids are now teenagers, and some days, I only see them for a half hour. Our grocery bill is three times our first mortgage. Our parents are in their 70s and now need more support from us than we need from them. I think I’m still in touch with modern culture, but my kids assure me I’m not. I may have 40-plus years left, but it sure feels like most of my life is now behind me. Most deeply, I’m frequently reflecting on life’s disappointments and griefs, wondering if I should have done this or that differently. This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Wilson, who writes specifically for men entering or inhabiting these decades, acknowledges all these challenges. “But,” he writes, “while this season presents unique challenges . . . midlife also presents exciting opportunities to trust Jesus for personal, marital, and spiritual flourishing” (xi). Thankfully, Wilson helps us reframe the demands and opportunities of middle age not as a necessary crisis but as a critical crossroads . Crossroads, Not Crisis For almost 60 years, pop culture has made “midlife” nearly synonymous with “crisis.” The phrase comes from psychoanalyst Elliott Jaques’s 1965 essay “ Death and the Mid-Life Crisis ” and has been repeated across dozens of books ever since. (There’s even a board game called Mid-Life Crisis, where players aim to accumulate wealth and avoid landing on bankruptcy, divorce, and nervous breakdown.) This is middle life. We’re too young to feel old. But we’re also too old to feel young. Fortunately, recent studies suggest fewer than 20 percent of Americans experience a full-on crisis in these middle decades. Despite this, many of us face a unique temptation to flee from responsibility or forge some entirely new life. Wilson puts it poignantly: “Whether you’re in a crisis or not, at midlife you’re at a crossroads” (16). At this crossroads, we see down one path the allure of individualism and freedom from responsibility. We might simply call this path the road of empty promises. As the proverbs say, it seems right, but in the end, it leads to death (Prov. 14:12). The second path is one of embracing reality, stepping deeper into relationship, and trusting the goodness of God. This road offers no promises other than the hardships of real life. But it’s also where we discover the true opportunity—giving our lives away to others. Wilson offers, “Maybe what [you need] in the second half is . . . a new vision, a renewed spirit of adventure and a commitment to do everything for the glory of God. . . . This is how you become great” (98). While the world may offer us the usual advice to build a life for ourselves, we know true happiness comes not in escaping relationships but prioritizing them. Even secular philosophers have discovered the most important rule of midlife is “to care about things other than yourself.” If this is true—and, of course, it comes originally from Jesus himself—then flourishing in midlife and across the second half should be about making the most of our relationships. If we can reject the path of empty promises and embrace the harder, more fruitful way of relationship, then we can begin to see middle age as a time to leave a meaningful legacy. Craft a Spiritual Legacy Paul wrote to the Corinthians: “You have countless guides in Christ, but you do not have many fathers” (1 Cor. 4:15). In the same way, most young men today have countless guides. From celebrity preachers to fitness influencers on YouTube, they have an unending source of content. But they don’t have many spiritual fathers. Wilson explains, The work of a spiritual fatherhood includes teaching, but more than that, it includes life-on-life investment, the sharing of quality time, the breaking of bread, and rejoicing and grieving with others. It means giving of ourselves to another, so that what is good and godly in us might pass along to them. The Lord uses our precious proximity to build up others. (137–38) At a time when we middle-aged men are wondering if our lives even matter, the possibility of leaving a spiritual legacy becomes invigorating. And, as Wilson shows us, it’s not about doing impressive and significant things before large crowds; it’s about having a deep influence on a few. A lifetime of steady faithfulness in relationships and responsibilities can be our gift to those closest to us. A lifetime of steady faithfulness in relationships and responsibilities can be our gift to those closest to us. My friends, this is good news. This season can be our best. We still have some energy and we’re gaining much wisdom. Of course, it isn’t easy. But within all the relationships and challenges lie this season’s greatest opportunity: finding our lives by giving them away. If we’re staring into the yawning chasm of middle age, the uncertainty and heaviness can lead us back to the graciousness of the Father, the friendship of Jesus, and the power of the Spirit. In Good News for Midlife , Jared Wilson reminds us to embrace our midlife crossroads, find new meaning in service to others, and let this season be an opportunity to discover grace upon grace in Jesus.

去年,我和一位二十多岁的学生坐在教堂里 他说他正在寻找一个年长的人来指导他,我开始通过我们的神明,智慧的人在50到60岁的时候思考. 他阻止了我,并澄清说: 他让我指导他 “等等,你以为我老了吗?” 我今年42岁,
有人大声问起我生下来是不是老了 我承认这个新奇的季节促使我去寻找智慧。 我将告诉你,读到中年是令人沮丧的。 根据研究,生活中的幸福遵循U形曲线. 我们自报的幸福始于童年时期,然后降入青春期,然后更早成年.
它在46岁左右的某个地方——在中世纪的中部——开始重新崛起,并稳步增长到我们的暮年。 此外,研究表明,抑郁症和焦虑症在45岁左右也最高. 尽管有各种坏消息,"中年的好消息:与古茨和格蕾丝一起导航中年"(Guts and Grace)是令人鼓舞的.
中西部浸信会神学院牧业部副教授Jared Wilson在50年代初写道,
多数人将“中年”定义为40至60岁, 对我来说,它看起来是这样的:我仍然感到精力充沛,但从失眠、受伤和旅行中恢复需要更长的时间。 我的孩子现在都是青少年 有些时候,我只看到他们半小时
我们的杂货单是我们第一次抵押贷款的三倍 我们的父母已经70多岁了 现在需要我们比他们更多的支持 但我的孩子向我保证我不是。 我可能还有40多年了 但感觉我大部分时间都过去了
我经常思考人生的失望和悲伤, 这是中间生活。 我们太年轻, 但我们也太老了, 威尔逊专门为进入或居住这几十年的男子写作,他承认所有这些挑战.
“不过,”他写道,“虽然这个季节提出了独特的挑战......中年也为相信耶稣的个人、婚姻和精神繁荣提供了令人兴奋的机会”(十一)。 值得庆幸的是,威尔逊帮助我们重新界定了中年的要求和机会,不是必要的危机,而是关键的十字路口。
十字路口,不是危机 近60年来,流行文化几乎把“中年”等同于“危机”。 这段话来自精神分析师艾略特·贾克斯1965年的论文“死亡与生活中期危机”,从此在数十本书中反复出现。
(甚至有一个名为“生活中危机”的棋盘游戏, 玩家的目标是积累财富, 这是中间生活。 我们太年轻, 但我们也太老了, 幸运的是,最近的研究表明,不到20%的美国人在这几十年中经历了一场全面危机。
尽管如此,我们许多人面临一种独特的诱惑,要逃避责任或创造一些全新的生活。 威尔逊强烈地说:“无论你是否处于危机之中, 在这个十字路口,我们看到一条道路是个人主义和免于责任的诱惑。 我们可能只是把这条道路称为空洞的承诺之路。
正如谚语所说,这似乎是正确的,但最终会导致死亡(Prov. 14:12). 第二条道路是拥抱现实,深入关系,相信上帝的善良. 这条路除了现实生活中的困难之外,没有其他的希望。 但这也是我们发现真正机会的地方,
威尔逊提出,“也许下半部分[你]需要的是......一种新的远见、新的冒险精神和为上帝的荣耀而做一切事情的承诺。 这就是你如何变得伟大”(98)。 虽然世界可能为我们提供通常的建议,为我们自己建立生活,但我们知道真正的幸福不是在逃避关系,而是在优先考虑关系。
甚至世俗哲学家也发现了中年最重要的规则是“关心你以外的事物”。 如果这是真的,当然,它来自耶稣本人,那么,在中年和下半年蓬勃发展,应该是为了充分利用我们的关系。
如果我们能够拒绝空洞的承诺,接受更艰难、更富有成效的关系方式,那么我们就可以开始将中年视为留下有意义的遗产的时刻。 保罗给科林斯人写了一封信:“你在基督中有无数的向导,但父亲并不多”(第4:15节)。 同样,今天大多数年轻人都有无数的向导。
从名人传教士到YouTube上的健身影响者,他们都有无限内容来源. 但是他们没有太多的灵性父亲。 威尔逊解释道, 灵父之作包括教义,但不止于此,还包括终身投资,分享优质时间,断面包,与他人共享快乐和悲伤.
这意味着要把自己交给另一个人,以便我们中善良和神圣的东西能够传给他们。 上帝利用我们珍贵的近距离 来建立其他人。 (137 -38) 正当我们中年男人想知道我们的生活是否重要的时候,留下精神遗产的可能性变得振奋人心.
正如威尔逊告诉我们的, 这并不是在大批人面前做令人印象深刻的重要事情; 而是对少数人产生深刻的影响。 一生在关系和责任方面坚定不移的忠诚,可以成为我们对最接近我们的人的礼物。 一生在关系和责任方面坚定不移的忠诚,可以成为我们对最接近我们的人的礼物。 朋友们,这是好消息。
这个季节可以是最好的。 我们还有些精力, 当然, 但这个季节最大的机会在于所有的关系和挑战,
若我们盯着中年的哈哈姆底沟看, 不确定和沉重会使我们回到父的仁慈、耶稣的友谊和灵的力量。 贾瑞德·威尔逊(Jared Wilson)提醒我们拥抱中年的十字路口, 在为他人服务时找到新的意义, 让这个季节成为在耶稣中发现恩典的机会。
